opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most interesting questions right now, because we're moving from software designed for humans to software that agents will also use, and maybe use mostly.

Today almost all software is built around a human sitting in front of a screen. You have buttons, menus, and dashboards, and the whole design assumes someone is looking, clicking and reading. Once agents become capable enough, a lot of that interface layer becomes less essential. An agent doesn't need a beautiful UI. It needs clear interfaces, reliable APIs, good documentation, and an environment where it can try things, get feedback, and recover from mistakes. So I think we'll see software gradually splitting into two layers. One layer is for agents: structured, programmable, verifiable. The other layer is for humans, and its role shifts from operating things to specifying intent and supervising results.

For people, that means the interaction becomes much more like delegation than operation. Instead of learning how to use ten different tools, you tell an agent what you want, and it figures out which tools to call and in what order. The skill that matters shifts from "do you know how to use Excel or Photoshop" to "can you describe your goal clearly, and can you judge whether the result is good." That's a big change. The bottleneck becomes taste and judgment rather than operational skill.

From a research perspective, especially coming from reinforcement learning, I think this also changes how software gets built. If agents are the main users, then software becomes an environment, and environments need to give good feedback signals. Right now a lot of software is very hard for agents to use, not because the models are dumb, but because the feedback is messy. Errors are ambiguous, states are hidden, and actions aren't reversible. I expect developers will start designing with agents in mind: clearer states, sandboxes, undo, verifiable outcomes. That makes agents much more reliable, and it also makes it possible to train them with RL directly on real tasks.

There's also a multi-agent dimension. Eventually you'll have agents talking to other agents, your agent negotiating with a service's agent, for example. Then questions like trust, permissions, and accountability become central. Who authorized this action? Can it be audited? I think a lot of the important work in the next few years won't only be about making models smarter. It'll be about building the infrastructure and the protocols so humans stay in control while agents do more of the actual work.

So my short answer is that software will become less about clicking and more about intent. Humans will set goals and check outcomes, and agents will handle execution. The companies and researchers who figure out that new interaction layer will define the next era of computing.

r001.rationale: The response says current software is designed for humans and describes agent-friendly APIs and environments, but it does not say GUI agents are needed.

r002.rationale: It explicitly predicts software will split into an agent layer and a human layer.

r003.rationale: It anticipates changes as agents become capable, but does not claim widespread AI adoption must happen before interaction models change.

r004.rationale: It describes people shifting toward stating goals and judging results, but does not suggest they will adapt to an interaction model AI already offers.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that a lot of software as we know it is going to stop being something you "use" and start being something that gets used on your behalf.

Right now almost every piece of software is designed around a human sitting in front of a screen. Menus, buttons, dashboards, settings pages. The whole interface exists to translate human intent into operations. But once agents become capable and widely deployed, the human increasingly expresses intent in natural language, and the agent is the one touching the software. So the interface that matters shifts from the UI to the API, to the tool layer, to whatever surface a model can read and act on reliably.

A few things follow from that.

First, I think we'll see a split between software built for humans and software built for agents. Some products will become thinner on the human side, almost like a status view, while the real work happens through programmatic interfaces that agents call. Other products that are inherently about human experience, games, creative tools, social things, will keep rich human interfaces, but even there an agent is likely sitting alongside you doing the tedious parts.

Second, the unit of software changes. Today you buy an app. In an agent world, you might buy a capability, and the agent assembles the pieces on the fly. The boundaries between products become less visible to the end user, because the agent is routing across them. That puts a lot of pressure on companies whose moat was the interface rather than the underlying capability or data.

Third, and this is the part I find most interesting from a research perspective, the interaction loop between humans and software gets longer and more delegated. Instead of click, see result, click again, you get: state a goal, agent works for minutes or hours, you review. That changes what reliability means. Small error rates that are fine when a human is checking every step become serious when the agent is taking hundreds of steps on its own. So a lot of the hard work is going to be in making agents trustworthy over long horizons, and in designing software that gives agents good feedback about whether they're doing the right thing.

And the last point, people's relationship to software itself changes. A lot of the skill of using software today is knowing where things are and how to make the tool do what you want. That skill becomes less valuable. What becomes more valuable is knowing what you actually want, being able to specify it clearly, and being able to judge whether the result is good. In some sense everyone becomes a manager of agents rather than an operator of tools.

I don't think this happens overnight, and I think the transition will be messier than the clean picture suggests. But the direction feels pretty clear to me.

r001.rationale: The response says current software is designed around human interfaces and describes agents using APIs or tools, but it does not explain that GUI agents are needed.

r002.rationale: It explicitly predicts a split between software built for humans and software built for agents, with different interface surfaces.

r003.rationale: It links the shift in interaction to agents becoming capable and widely deployed, presenting that adoption as a condition for the change.

r004.rationale: It says people will become more like managers of agents, but does not suggest they may adapt to an interaction model AI already offers.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that software will increasingly be used by agents on our behalf. Today, if you want to do something, you open an app, learn its interface, and go through a sequence of steps. With an agent, you can describe the outcome you want, and the agent can work across several applications to get there.

That changes what a good software interface looks like. You still need an interface for people, but you also need a reliable way for agents to understand what the software can do, take actions, and verify the results. A workflow that’s easy for a person to navigate visually isn’t necessarily easy for an agent to execute reliably.

And I think the human role shifts toward setting goals and supervising. The interesting question becomes: when should the agent act independently, and when should it come back and ask you? If it asks about every click, it hasn’t saved you much work. If it makes consequential decisions without checking, you won’t trust it. Getting that balance right will be a big part of making this useful.

r001.rationale: The response says today’s software workflows are built around people navigating app interfaces, while agents need a reliable way to understand and operate software. This communicates that existing software interfaces were not designed for agent use.

r002.rationale: It says software needs an interface for people and a separate reliable way for agents to understand capabilities and take actions, raising the possibility of distinct interaction surfaces.

r003.rationale: The response describes how software use may change as agents become more common, but does not claim that widespread AI adoption must happen before interaction models change.

r004.rationale: The response discusses agents adapting to software and people setting goals or supervising; it does not suggest people may adapt to an interaction model AI already offers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that software will increasingly be used by agents on behalf of people. Today, we learn an application’s interface: where to click, which fields to fill in, how to move information from one tool to another. With capable AI agents, you can describe what you want to accomplish, and the agent can handle some of those steps across applications.

That could change how we build software, too. An application would need to serve both human users and agents, with clear ways to access information, take actions, and check the results. The human interface might become more focused on expressing intent, reviewing proposed actions, and handling exceptions.

But delegation requires trust. If an agent misunderstands you, a small mistake can propagate across several tools. So I think permissions, visibility, and the ability to undo actions will become central to the experience. The interesting question is how much people can comfortably delegate while still understanding and controlling what happens.

r001.rationale: The response says applications should serve agents as well as people, but does not explain that GUI agents are needed because existing software was not designed for AI use.

r002.rationale: It describes applications serving both human users and agents, with a human interface focused on intent, review, and exceptions, conveying distinct interaction paths for each.

r003.rationale: The response does not claim that AI must become widely adopted before interaction models change.

r004.rationale: The response does not suggest that people may adapt to the interaction model AI already offers.
